To compute ${g}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u={e}^{x}$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{{e}^{x}}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(-{\int }_{5}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{5}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{5}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡({t}^{3})\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡({u}^{3})) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(({e}^{x})^{3})) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{3x}).\end{aligned}
$$
